name: Escanaba Gateway
description:
Escanaba occupies the UP's southern shore, facing Lake Michigan across Little Bay de Noc, and its function is exactly what the name suggests: it is the gateway. The port handles the ore, timber, and manufactured goods that flow south from the UP's interior to the markets and mills of the lower Great Lakes. Kelpline Logistics operates the port facilities under a sovereignty charter, and the automated cargo handling systems move tonnage 24 hours a day through a facility that was built for ten times the human workforce it currently employs. The port is efficient, profitable, and nearly empty of people — the automation revolution hit Escanaba harder than anywhere else in the UP, replacing dock workers with systems that don't take breaks, don't form unions, and don't spend money in local bars.

The result is a city that processes enormous wealth and retains almost none of it. The ore comes down from Marquette and Iron Mountain. The timber comes down from the northern forests. The finished materials come from Copperhead's fabrication facilities. All of it passes through Escanaba's port, loaded onto lake barges bound for GLMZ, The Lattice, and points south. The city takes its cut — port fees, maintenance contracts, fuel sales — but the cut is thin and getting thinner as automation reduces the human infrastructure required to move cargo. The residential population has been declining for two decades, and the downtown district has the particular emptiness of a place that was built for more people than currently inhabit it.

Escanaba's strategic value in the UP war lies in its position. Control the southern port and you control the UP's economic output. Michigan holds it. Wisconsin wants it. The Mackinac Bridge — 150 kilometers east — is the only other route south from the UP, and it's a chokepoint, not a port. Whoever holds Escanaba can starve the UP or feed it, which makes the city's small population disproportionately important and disproportionately nervous.

sights: Automated cargo cranes operating on the port — massive, precise, and eerily unmanned
Empty storefronts on Ludington Street — the downtown built for a population that left
Lake Michigan visible from everywhere — blue-grey and busy with cargo barge traffic
Kelpline Logistics sovereign territory markers along the waterfront — corporate authority over public shore
The ore trains arriving from the interior, loaded cars stretching to the horizon
sounds: Automated port operations — the whir and clank of machines handling cargo without human direction
Wind off Lake Michigan — steady, cold, and carrying the sound of barge traffic
The absence of crowds — Escanaba's streets are quiet in a way that feels like a warning
Ore trains arriving and departing — the rhythm of extraction moving through the city like a pulse
smells: Lake Michigan air — cleaner than Superior, warmer, carrying a different mineral profile
Iron ore dust from the transit operations — the UP's export made visible and breathable
Diesel and electric motor exhaust from the cargo handling systems
atmosphere.feel: A city that serves a function and wonders if the function will continue to need a city. Escanaba works, but it works the way a machine works — efficiently, impersonally, and without any particular attachment to the people who live alongside it. The emptiness is not desolate. It is procedural.

demographics: Population 18,000, down from 35,000 two decades ago. The decline tracks automation adoption almost exactly. The remaining population is predominantly port support workers, Kelpline employees, and the businesses that serve them. Median age is rising. Young people leave for Iron Crown or the lower peninsula. The ones who stay have reasons.
economy: Port operations (Kelpline Logistics) and cargo transit. Escanaba is a throughput economy — value passes through without accumulating. The city's GDP per capita is technically high; the city's livability is technically declining. The automation dividend goes to Kelpline shareholders, not to Escanaba residents.
power_structure: Kelpline Logistics holds port sovereignty. Michigan municipal government holds residential jurisdiction. The practical power balance is determined by employment — Kelpline employs 40% of the remaining workforce directly, and another 30% indirectly. The mayor governs at Kelpline's convenience.
dangers: Economic obsolescence — automation is reducing the human workforce required, and the trend has no floor
Strategic vulnerability — the port is a high-value target in the UP war, and the population is too small to defend it
Kelpline workforce reductions — each round of automation eliminates jobs that don't come back
Wisconsin-aligned sabotage of port operations — disrupting southern shipping to weaken Michigan's economic position
The psychological toll of living in a shrinking city — Escanaba's mental health infrastructure is as understaffed as everything else
opportunities: Port access — Escanaba is the gateway to southern markets, and access has value
Automation systems expertise — the port's technology is state-of-the-art, and technicians who maintain it are employable everywhere
Strategic intelligence — shipping manifests from Escanaba reveal the UP's economic activity in real time
Real estate — the depopulation has made property cheap, which attracts certain kinds of operations that prefer low visibility
story_hooks: Kelpline Logistics is negotiating a 'security partnership' with Wisconsin that would effectively surrender the port without Michigan's consent
Automated cargo containers are being loaded with unmanifested materials at night — the port's own systems are being used to smuggle something south
A Wisconsin military force is staging 80 kilometers west, and the only thing between them and Escanaba is forest and a population too small to matter

adjacent_to: Iron Crown (Marquette, north along the UP corridor)
Ironvein (Iron Mountain, northwest along the border zone)
The Mackinac Bridge (east, connecting to the lower peninsula)
GLMZ (south across Lake Michigan, via cargo barge routes)

frequented_by: Kelpline Logistics personnel and port automation technicians
Cargo barge crews transiting to southern markets
Michigan military observers monitoring the Wisconsin border
The shrinking community of permanent residents who haven't left yet
